newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks said to use gangster for missions abroad.
newsitem.headline: Turks said to use gangster for missions abroad.

text.p: A scandal over Turkey's alleged use of gangsters as political hitmen deepened on Friday after official testimony that a drug smuggler wanted for murder had carried out missions abroad for the security establishment.
Former interior ministry adviser Korkut Eken told a parliamentary inquiry that far-right mobster Abdullah Catli had worked with security officials for years, parliamentary sources said.
"He said he knew Catli and that (the gangster) had worked for the state, even before 1980," a source close to the commission of inquiry told Reuters.
A top intelligence officer told the same inquiry on Thursday that Turkey's intelligence service MIT had cooperated with Catli in unspecified foreign ventures in the 1980s, the source said.
It was the strongest confirmation of media and opposition reports that leading officials were closely linked to underworld figures in the past. The reports say the links may still exist.

Catli is central to a scandal that erupted on November 3 when he died in a traffic accident as a passenger in a car also carrying a senior policeman and a government MP from Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller's True Path Party.

The interior minister, also from Ciller's party, quit last month amid accusations that Turkish officials used gangsters into the 1990s to kill Kurdish rebel sympathisers and business rivals in exchange for ignoring gangland drug smuggling and money laundering.
Ciller told members of a crack police unit not to be demoralised by accusations that some of its members were embroiled in illegal killings and the drugs trade.
"There have been unjustified attacks against you recently. I know how much that has saddened you," Ciller said in an address to a police academy near Ankara.

"Keep your heads up high," said Ciller, dressed in a camouflage special forces jacket. Three members of the unit have been suspended for allegedly cooperating with Catli in the July murder of Turkey's top casino owner in a drug money quarrel.

The Islamist-led coalition government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has shown few signs of cracking in the face of media reports that Ciller's businessman husband and several members of her party are close to the mob.
Pro-Islam backbench MPs are uneasy about a speech last month by conservative Ciller in which she indirectly praised Catli as a patriot.
Catli, a member of the extreme-right Grey Wolves movement, was wanted for the killing of seven Turkish leftists in 1978.

Parliamentary sources confirmed reports in several dailies that the head of Turkish intelligence's anti-terror unit, Mehmet Eymur, testified on Thursday that the intelligence service had worked with Catli.

"He told the commission that the state used Abdullah Catli abroad from 1983," Islamist deputy Mehmet Elkatmis, who chairs the parliamentary inquiry, told the ATV television station. He did not specify what tasks Catli may have carried out.
Catli spent time in jail in France and Switzerland for drug smuggling in the 1980s. A forged version of a type of passport given only to leading officials was found on his body after the car crash.
The Turkish media have said Catli was involved in the killing of Armenian guerrilla leader Agop Agopian in Athens in 1988.
Eymur told the commission the intelligence service cut its relation with Catli when it became aware of his drug dealings.
"We gave him up and national police headquarters took him and began to use him," Hurriyet newspaper quoted Eymur as saying. The inquiry is closed to the press but there have been frequent leaks.
